item.title: Iran says 'ball is in the U.S. court' on any deal to end the war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What to know about the Iran war today: Mediators continue pushing for a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the eight-month war sparked by U.S. and Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic. Three consecutive days of indirect, closed-door negotiations led by Qatar have yielded no apparent breakthrough, with Iran saying Monday that "the ball is in the U.S. court."President Trump has kept his intentions on Iran ambiguous, saying Saturday that the U.S. still has targets to "take care of," and then telling a radio network on Sunday that the war will soon be over "one way or the other … either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it."Mr. Trump told reporters he had a "very good talk" Sunday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, discussing the Iran war. Sources quoted by Axios said the president wants to let negotiations play out, while Netanyahu is pushing to resume strikes on Iran. Oil prices drop roughly 7% ahead of U.S. midterm elections Oil prices sank around seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the U.S., as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war. Earlier, Axios outlet reported that Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, in the highest-level move from the Trump administration in months. Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management, told AFP that her organization believes such signals from the administration "may be tactical" ahead of the midterms. "Meanwhile, attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz continue [and] we maintain our higher-for-longer outlook for energy prices," Rasmussen said. But share prices of energy majors have dropped, while many other sectors were boosted by the cooling fuel costs. Stocks got a lift from sharp drops in oil prices, which headed back down in their latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 7.4% to $105.03. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war began, and it's been quick to reverse direction. AP/AFP Houthi spokesperson says Saudi coalition launched more than 100 strikes since Sunday Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthis, said Monday that the Saudi coalition fighting the rebel group in Yemen had launched more than 100 airstrikes over the course of the last day. "Saudi warplanes launched 109 airstrikes over the past 24 hours," the spokesperson said in a statement shared on X. The strikes targeted the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf, and Hodeidah, according to the statement. Some of those provinces are in Houthi-controlled or contested territories. The spokesperson said airstrikes between Sunday and Monday brought the total number of Saudi strikes and missile attacks to 3,939 since the fighting in Yemen escalated earlier this fall. Saree's latest comments came after he claimed in another statement Monday that the Houthis had carried out new attacks against Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport, over the last 48 hours. Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airport, military assets A spokesman for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed Monday that the group had carried out new attacks over the preceding 48 hours on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, said in a statement shared on social media that the group had struck Saudi Arabia's eastern Dammam Airport "using two drones, and the operation achieved its objective successfully, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport." He said another drone hit an "early warning radar in Jizan," a city on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast, while unspecified Houthi weapons hit "a military transport aircraft at Jizan Airport." The Houthis have peppered Saudi Arabia's airports and energy infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of Yemen's government in the impoverished Middle Eastern nation's grueling decade-long civil war. Iran has long backed the Houthis as a powerful proxy force, particularly as a counter to Iran's arch-foe Saudi Arabia, which shares a long border with Yemen. Houthi drone and missile strikes last month killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports , and despite the kingdom's vast military and financial advantage over the rebels, it has been unable to stop the attacks . There was no immediate information from Saudi officials to confirm or deny Saree's claims on Monday. Senior Iranian official thanks Putin, talks "strategic cooperation" in phone call with Russian leader The Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday, Iranian state media reported, in a continuation of recent talks between the two countries about the situation in the Middle East. During their call, Rezaei and Putin discussed regional and global affairs, focusing on West Asia and ongoing "strategic cooperation" between Iran and Russia, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency. Iran and Russia have long been allies, and their relationship has been cemented during both the ongoing Russian assault on Ukraine, and the U.S. war with Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in October that Tehran's ties with Russia were closer than ever, contradicting Mr. Trump's assertion at the time that Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Tehran amid the war. According to Tasnim, Rezaei thanked Putin Monday for Russia's support. Iran's top diplomat says negotiations "proceeding very intensively," but "everything depends on" U.S. side Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. "If they choose honest diplomacy, we are ready to engage," IRNA quoted Araghchi as saying. "If they intend to deceive us and launch military operations, they will face a response more bitter and forceful than before." Another tanker on fire near Strait of Hormuz after hitting sea mine, Iranian news agency claims The Iranian Navy claimed Monday that another oil tanker had caught on fire after striking a sea mine near the eastern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, which is closely linked with Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The report cited the Navy as saying the unnamed vessel had struck a mine while attempting to use shipping lanes through the strait that Iran considers unauthorized and unsafe, but which the Trump administration and U.S. military have repeatedly claimed are free and open. The tanker had switched off its navigation systems, Fars said, referring to a common practice by commercial vessels trying to obscure their movements in the region. Tanker owners should take a lesson from the fate of vessels that violate Iran's rules by trying to transit the strait without authorization from Tehran, the report cited the navy as saying. On Friday, despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that the southern shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe to navigate, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in the month of October alone, a record high. The Iranian regime said earlier Monday that 11 ships had "caught fire" in or near the Strait of Hormuz in the last nine days alone. Iran says it proposed shorter 2-day implementation period for proposed peace deal with U.S. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran had presented Qatari mediators with a proposal to shorten the implementation period of a potential deal with the U.S. to just two days from seven. In an interview with Al Jazeera , Araghchi said: "The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days." The Iranian minister added, however, that Tehran's conditions for a deal to end the war remain the same. The Islamic Republic regime has demanded that the U.S. release frozen Iranian financial assets, lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as sanctions, and cease hostilities on all fronts, including Israel's battle with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. In exchange, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping traffic and commit to further talks on its nuclear program. Under the original seven-day implementation proposed by Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz would have been reopened on the sixth day. With the shortened implementation period, according to a statement on the Iranian government website, "a series of measures will be taken by the United States on the first day, and on the second day, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and maritime traffic will return to its previous conditions." Iran claims 11 tankers "caught fire" in 9 days as U.S. commander declared Strait of Hormuz "free and clear" Iran's government-run broadcaster IRIB said Monday that 11 oil tankers had "caught fire" in the Strait of Hormuz in the previous nine days, disputing U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper's assertion last week that "all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear." In a post on X, IRIB said the 11 tankers had caught on fire since Oct. 25, the day on which it claimed Cooper made his recent fly-over of the strait. The Iranian network offered no evidence, but claimed some of the vessels sank "to the depths of the sea." Since the start of the war in February, Iran has targeted vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to assert control over the narrow waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's crude oil supply typically passed prior to the conflict. Cooper said last week in a Friday video statement that he saw no Iranian navy vessels in the strait during his flyover earlier in the week. Later Friday, however, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the month of October alone, a record high. The U.S. military and President Trump have repeatedly declared Iran's navy destroyed and insisted that southern shipping lanes through the strait are available to merchant vessels, but ongoing Iranian threats and attacks have kept the risks and costs for shippers high, which has helped Tehran keep maintain pressure on global energy prices. Iran again warns of natural gas shortages ahead of winter Iranian officials repeated warnings Monday of possible gas shortages for residents ahead of the winter, and they called on people to conserve the resource. First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said he had to be honest about the stability of Iran's gas network in the colder months, as he asked the public to help conserve it. Aref cited "imbalances accumulated over previous years and war-related damages," and warned that prices would increase for consumers who fail to conserve. It is not the first time an Iranian official has warned about shortages. On October 25 , Iran's parliament speaker said natural gas consumption across Iran had to be reduced by 10%. Iran's economy has been devastated by years of international sanctions, and the U.S. turn to economic warfare after the initial bombing campaigns of the ongoing conflict have strained finances for Tehran even further. The regime has not shown any willingness to bend on its demands to end the war, however, despite the economic pain for most Iranians. Iran says the "ball is in the U.S. court" on any prospective peace deal Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make. "The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran. Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics. President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war. Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other." "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context. Netanyahu reportedly pushes for new U.S. strikes on Iran President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him." Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran. According to sources cited by Axios , Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out. The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated. Mr. Trump has repeatedly hinted he is considering resuming attacks on Iran after the midterm elections. Push for U.S.-Iran deal shadowed by threats to resume fighting Qatari mediators are leading indirect talks aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran, but the closed door negotiations have been punctuated by exchanges of threats between the leaders of both countries. Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who added the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States. On Saturday, President Trump said the U.S. still had to "take care of" one or two more potential targets in Iran, citing a suspected nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain. On Sunday he reiterated the threat, saying he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time. Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday there would be no "geographical limitations" should the fighting with the U.S. resume, adding that there is a "vast theatre" to inflict damage. Both sides have previously acknowledged that indirect talks are underway but consistently exchange threats. CBS/AFP UAE hopes for diplomacy but braces for "the worst" The United Arab Emirates' presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible, but that they are also preparing for the possibility of escalation. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Anwar Gargash said Iran's attacks on Gulf countries such as the UAE made this a "watershed year" for the region. "We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," Gargash told the audience. But he added that his country and the region are braced for the "the worst," referring to the resumption of active hostilities. The UAE was consistently targeted by Tehran in the opening weeks of the war in retribution for U.S. strikes on Iran, disrupting tourism and daily life, and effectively throwing the security landscape of the region into question. CBS/AP Vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. maritime agency says A vessel was struck on Sunday by "an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime security agency said, after Qatari media reported an earlier attack on a gas tanker. Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait. Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said. The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said. Since the Middle East war began in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping. Trump says war in Iran will be put away "very soon, one way or the other" President Trump said he believes the U.S. will soon put the war with Iran away, "one way or the other." The president was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr. Trump said. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it… The job we've done is amazing." Earlier Sunday, Iran's top diplomat said he hopes there is "rationality" on the U.S. side as diplomatic efforts seek to avert a return to all-out war. item.title: Democrats eye a return to power. Division over how to handle Trump is already brewing.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats are expecting to win big on Election Day, but disagreements are already erupting among them over how aggressively to target President Trump for what they say are abuses of power and corruption. Democratic lawmakers and strategists are divided over whether to push another impeachment against Trump. Senators and leaders in the House are generally opposed to advancing a third impeachment of Trump that has virtually no chance of picking up 67 votes in the Senate — the number of votes needed to convict. A senior Senate Democratic aide warned there is little “appetite” for holding a third Trump impeachment trial in the Senate, after previous impeachment efforts in 2020 and 2021 failed to impact Trump politically. Democrats agree there need to be investigations of Trump and his allies next year to hold them to account, but there is little consensus over what to prioritize, according to Democratic strategists and aides. But some senior lawmakers are warning that the party can’t get so wrapped up in tracking down the misdeeds of the president and the administration that they get pulled into too many directions or lose sight of addressing high prices and ending the war in Iran — two of the top issues of this year’s election. “I don’t think we can ignore it,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) of the need to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration. “More than 90 percent of voters think that government has been corrupted. We just have to be thoughtful and strategic about where investigative work goes and not allow that to distract us from solving fairly immediate cost problems that American families feel,” he said. Whitehouse would become chair of the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate. To keep their hoped-for new House majority — and possible Senate majority — from getting sucked into solely partisan battles with Trump over what has already transpired, Democratic leaders in Congress are mapping out positive agendas for the first 100 hours, the first 100 days and the first year of their new majorities, according to sources familiar with internal discussions. Yet the desire among Democratic lawmakers to inflict retribution on Trump is strong. Some want to delve further into the Jeffrey Epstein sex-trafficking scandal to probe whether the Justice Department violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act by withholding or improperly redacting documents. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who would return to the role of majority leader if Democrats capture the Senate, created a special Senate working group in February to plumb Epstein-related information held back from the public by the Trump Justice Department. “We are demanding that the Department of Justice and the FBI preserve records on what transpired behind the scenes. We want to know who was involved in the decision to hide the truth,” he declared. Other Democrats want to prioritize investigations of the Defense Department and the awarding of lucrative contracts linked to Donald Trump Jr. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth earlier this year demanding information about decisions at the Pentagon to give loans and contracts to companies “associated with the president’s son” that may have had “conflicts of interest.” Some Democrats are pushing for investigations into the Trump family’s massive investments in the crypto industry; the president’s pardon of Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, who pleaded guilty to violating money laundering law; and whether crypto investments provided an avenue for foreign interests to influence the president. “We’re going to have to do voluminous oversight work because there is rampant corruption in this administration, and we need to get to the bottom of it,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.). Some Democrats want to investigate Trump’s pardon record more closely and scrutinize donations that wealthy individuals and families made in hopes of receiving clemency. The New York Times reported that Alina Habba Mildon, one of Trump’s former lawyers, earned $50 million to help secure a pardon for the member of a wealthy Venezuelan family, among other duties. A Democratic strategist and former House leadership aide said Democratic leaders are looking at a wide array of issues to investigate when they take back the Speaker’s gavel in January. “Everything from corporate America and their ties to the Trump administration, Epstein, immigration,” said the strategist, noting that Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who would take over as chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has been outspoken about investigating conditions at Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities and immigration enforcement activities more generally. “They’re going to spend their time looking at a variety of issues,” the strategist added, noting Democrats are “running on affordability and corruption” in the midterm election. The House-aligned Democratic strategist said there’s little desire among House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries's (N.Y.) leadership team to move toward another impeachment proceeding, even though there are rank-and-file members in the Democratic caucus who want to. “I’ll tell you right now that I have not heard about impeachment, not for Trump,” the source said. The strategist said Democratic leaders instead are eyeing a lower-key strategy to hamstring the Trump administration by tying up Cabinet and other senior officials in oversight hearings. “That’s what they’re elected to do, to constrain Trump and to ensure that they try to get some of their agenda passed and signed into law,” the strategist said. Beyond investigations, Democrats are threatening to make it much tougher for Trump to make appointments to the federal judiciary and the executive branch if they win control of the Senate. And they’ve threatened to cut off funding for the war with Iran if Trump doesn’t bring the conflict to a swift conclusion. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is set to become the next Senate Democratic whip, has warned that getting bipartisan majorities to vote for bills to authorize and fund the Pentagon will be “extremely difficult” if the war drags on. Some Democrats, however, argue that Trump still needs to face accountability for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election or for mishandling classified documents and conspiring to obstruct justice related to those documents after leaving office in 2021. “Donald Trump’s alleged crimes still have not been given justice. There’s been no justice yet for these alleged crimes, which are just so deeply serious, and were stopped midway in the criminal justice process,” said Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee. “I still feel there needs to be some reckoning,” he said. Blumenthal would be poised to take over as chair of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations if Democrats win control of the Senate this week. Other Democrats say they want to investigate what they say has been a “corrupt relationship” between the Trump administration and wealthy special interests over the past 20 months. Murphy says he wants to know more about “an $8 million donation made by R.J. Reynolds to the administration that resulted one week later in flavored vapes being made legal for kids.” “We should get to the bottom of the corrupt relationship that exists between corporations in this country and the Trump administration,” he said. item.title: Republicans privately criticize Trump amid fears of major midterm election losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans are already privately blaming President Donald Trump as they brace for losses on Tuesday. Even as they race to distance themselves from his actions on tariffs, the unpopular Iran war and his mass deportation agenda, few have been willing to criticize him publicly — a clear sign of just how powerful Trump's grip remains on the GOP. But interviews with roughly a dozen candidates, campaign officials and lawmakers reveal they're acutely aware of who, exactly, put them on the back foot this entire cycle. "There was a point earlier this year where we really felt like we could defy history," said one House Republican, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to candidly discuss midterms dynamics. "And then Trump bombed Iran. And it was just one thing after another.” Republicans are tied or trailing in polls in numerous critical battlegrounds and expecting to lose some once-secure red seats. And Trump's unfocused closing message — including repeated comments about male candidates' physical appearances — has further frustrated an already on-edge party. “I think Jon Husted's ass and Nicki Minaj's is a great closing message,” T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist working on the South Carolina Senate race and others, said sarcastically in an interview on The Conversation with Dasha Burns . “You’ve got to take the good with the bad with Trump, unless you want to drive yourself crazy every day.” “People are gonna go after the president. The buck stops with him. His approval ratings aren't great,” he added. Privately, some Republicans are even harsher. “At least when Barack Obama was president, he only screwed his enemies, never his friends,” said a second House Republican. The White House defended its involvement in the war with Iran, tariff regime and approach to immigration enforcement. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Trump “is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” One White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the blame game “an asinine adventure” and said Trump “has obviously left it all on the field.” If the bottom falls out for the GOP on Tuesday, the quiet calls assigning him blame may turn into a public shanking as Trump nears the lame-duck stage of his presidency, Republicans refocus on how to win voters back for 2028 and jostle for their own spots in the party’s future. “I'm not sure what the Republican Party looks like in six months. Look, a lot of Republicans have held their tongues. A lot of Republicans who have real problems with the way things have gone the last two years have been good soldiers,” said a Republican strategist involved in competitive midterm races across the country. “But what happens if we lose 35 House seats and six Senate seats?” “We all know who the problem is. It’s Trump. And do we continue down a path of losing?” the strategist added. In Georgia, some Republicans have already warned that low early voting turnout in rural parts of the state could drag down their entire ticket. "If you live in rural Georgia, you're going to be disproportionately hurt by higher — especially diesel — prices,” said Jason Shepherd, the former GOP chair of suburban Cobb County. “The promise of the great Trump economy has not materialized." Top Hill Republicans have worked behind the scenes for months to try to alleviate some of the political fallout from Trump’s election year policy moves, including arguing to White House officials that Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers could lose their races if the administration didn’t reach an off-ramp from the trade war with Canada, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the matter. Eventually, Trump agreed to roll back some tariffs and add new ones in a boost to Collins. Republicans also pressed for the White House to undo some of Trump’s other controversial moves, like his executive order to import more foreign beef that has riled ranchers and farmers in red states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas. But that relief never came. "Republicans have always been aware of the historical midterm precedent, and that's why we're barnstorming the country to tout the president's achievements on cutting taxes, securing the border, and lowering drug costs,” said Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. “Any anonymous strategist who says the president is not helpful in turning out Republican voters has no idea what they're talking about, and their candidates should request a refund for their shoddy consulting services." But Trump’s actions, Republicans say, are hitting different parts of the country hard. The Iran war, they argue, was a significant blunder from Trump that has multiplied Democrats’ paths to power in both the House and Senate by driving fuel and fertilizer costs up — most notably impacting races across the Midwest. The White House’s tariffs regime has been a major concern in battlegrounds on the Canadian border like Maine and Michigan. Hardline immigration enforcement that has resulted in the deportation of thousands has hurt especially in heavily Latino border states like Arizona and Texas, and the cancelling of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Venezuelans has enraged South Florida voters. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Miami Republican, warned the president in a campaign ad earlier this year that his immigration tactics had gone too far. “Trump won Miami, and yet he went to the place that gave him the biggest support, and kind of just fucked everybody over if we're being honest.” said one Florida-based Republican operative. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Republican midterm voters are split over who they would blame if the GOP performs worse than it did in 2024: A sizable 29% blame Trump for making the GOP less popular, while 30% said it is because Trump himself is not on the ballot. Fourteen percent said it would be because the Democratic Party has become more popular, while roughly one in four said they don’t know. Some in the party question whether Trump’s last-minute campaign travel across the country and the millions of dollars his political operation has poured into battleground states will even be enough. They see him as more absorbed in protecting his legacy than making actionable policy changes to help his party stay in power. “He cares more about the ballroom than he cares about Republicans winning the midterms,” said a third Republican strategist working in battleground races. “He wants the Nobel Peace Prize, these big legacy-defining things seem to be taking up more of his attention than actually being president.” A fourth GOP operative working on midterms races has a curt message if Republicans lose big: “Thank you, Donald Trump." item.title: Which party has a better chance of winning the midterms? What the final polls say.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are tomorrow. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is almost up — and the stakes on Nov. 3 couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape has reached its final form — and the polling trends are clear. Here are the numbers on the eve of Election Day. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after nearly two years of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.5 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot. The next day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by the eve of Election Day, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 8.7 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University poll shows Jackson ahead by 6 . Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Eighteen polls were conducted in October. Seventeen of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 9 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives El-Sayed an 11-point lead ; new polls from YouGov ( El-Sayed +4 ) and Research Co. ( El-Sayed +2 ) show smaller margins for the Democrat. Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives Brown a 6-point advantage . Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . A new Echelon Insights survey gives Ossoff a 15-point lead . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 11 points, on average . Final polls from YouGov and East Carolina University show him ahead by 11 points and 9 points, respectively. New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7.5 percentage points — over the last month. The final University of New Hampshire survey shows him ahead by 12 . Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena Universty poll gives her a narrow 48-46% advantage . Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . The final YouGov and New York Times/Siena University polls show Turek ahead by 1 point; GrayHouse and co/efficient polls show Hinson leading by 2. Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins were small — between 2 and 6 points. But the Democrat seems to be closing strong: final polls from Atlas Intel and the New York Times/Siena University show him ahead by 6 and 7 points, respectively. Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Ricketts ahead by 1 point; a New York Times/Siena University survey released on Saturday gives Ricketts a 6-point lead. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say : Only one survey conducted over the last month shows Marshall ahead (by a single point). The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). A new CNN poll has Hamilton up by 4 ; a new Emerson College survey puts him ahead by roughly the same amount . On Friday, the Washington Post released a poll showing Hamilton lapping Marshall by about 10 points. But the paper questioned its own results , noting that Republicans responded at much lower rates than Democrats. The final New York Times/Siena University survey shows Hamilton ahead by 5 . South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham held a narrow lead in most fall surveys . But it was small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Friday gave Andrews a 5-point advantage; a new New York Times/Siena University poll shows the two candidates essentially tied. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -21.5% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. item.title: Trump admin. appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 mail ballots in California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections . The emergency appeal came after a divided appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens . The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters’ status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens. The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare. A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress. The Justice Department asked the high court for a “limited injunction” that would direct California to set aside the ballots while the case plays out. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.” The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early. Trump's administration has racked up a series of wins in emergency appeals before the Supreme Court in his second term, but the justices previously rejected the president’s push to restrict mail ballots ahead of the midterms. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court . item.title: Man completes 31,000-mile walk around the world and returns to mom’s house
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world . “Where have you been?” his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.” He didn’t need to tell her. Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward. He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders. A trek made possible by kind strangers On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero’s welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother. “Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. “Is that it, is it done?” The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother's rowhouse at the age of 29. He returned as a 57-year-old — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly. “They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” The idea started with a birthday card from his dad Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. “You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.” Danger on land and sea followed by border problems He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month. He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time. Bushby hadn't seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew. “Behave yourself, mother,” he joked, as his mother wept and he held her and rubbed her back. “Get yourself together.” In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, living in his mom's basement and not knowing what he would do. “It’s like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole,” he told The Associated Press. “I have no idea what’s about to happen in my life.” ___ Melley reported from London. item.title: Prosecutors announce intention to retry Lindsay Clancy for deaths of her 3 children
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Prosecutors announced in court on Nov. 2 that they intend to retry Lindsay Clancy , the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children. Clancy, 36, was charged with murder for killing her children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on Jan. 24, 2023, by strangling them with exercise bands in the basement of their Duxbury home. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued she can't be held criminally responsible, Massachusetts' version of the insanity defense, because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Clancy's triple murder trial ended with a hung jury in early September, leaving her fate in limbo. Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors want to retry Clancy but are waiting to decide what charges she will face until Judge William Sullivan makes a decision on three motions, including a defense motion to dismiss the murder charges. "Your honor, this would be a retrial. As to what that looks like will depend," Sprague said. "We're not at that point yet." Reddington argued prosecutors don't need to know the outcome of the motions to determine what charges they will retry Clancy on. "Why do we not know if the next trial will be murder in the first degree, or a lesser charge or no charge?" he asked. Reddington said he wants Sullivan, who is approaching mandatory retirement in June, to preside over the trial in the spring. Sullivan said requested the parties appear on Nov. 16 for another hearing. If Sullivan dismisses the defense's motion to dismiss at that hearing, the parties will then select a trial date, which Sullivan said he is hoping to schedule in March. Judge to weigh motion to dismiss The defense team pushed to have the charges against Clancy dismissed altogether and launch an investigation into the holdout juror. Defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued on Nov. 2 that retrying Clancy would violate constitutional protections against double jeopardy because Sullivan should have questioned the jury more thoroughly after receiving notes indicating one juror was refusing to follow the court's instruction on reasonable doubt, an allegation the holdout juror has denied . Sullivan interjected, noting he did question the jurors individually before declaring a mistrial on Sept. 4. Weinberg said the question Sullivan asked was “simply constitutionally insufficient to probe what was going on in that jury room." Prosecutors opposed the defense's motion , saying the mistrial was properly declared after the jury repeatedly reported it was deadlocked. Sprague argued that Sullivan could not have questioned the jurors further without probing the substance of deliberations, which is prohibited, and even if he could have done so, the appropriate response wouldn’t be dismissing the charges. "It’s not for the trial judge to choose sides in a deadlocked jury and decide," she said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Reddington asked the court to question the juror about the truthfulness of a questionnaire and his answers during jury selection, a "sworn assurance" from Sept. 3, and the use of a cell phone or receipt of outside information during deliberations. In a fiery exchange on Nov. 2, Reddington said he has evidence the holdout juror was using his cellphone and researching altruistic filicide during deliberations. Reddington said the juror was also dishonest about his criminal history on his questionnaire. Heather O'Connor, an attorney for the holdout juror, said that the mistrial decision had to be made based on what was known at the time and that these allegations came to light after the jury was dismissed. "And to be clear Juror Doe does not concede any of those allegations," O'Connor said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Prosecutors push for gag order Prosecutors also asked the court to prohibit defense attorneys, as well as themselves, from speaking to the media in a way that would "have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceedings." Sprague argued Reddington has already made many statements that were inappropriate and "calculated to affect the public's perception of the case," including asking for a presidential pardon and saying the other jurors were "robbed" by the holdout. A defense attorney opposed that motion, arguing that such an order would constitute "prior restraint" of speech that infringes upon both Reddington's and Clancy's First Amendment rights. They said that no trial date had been set and the impact of these alleged comments on a potential future jury is "merely speculative." Sullivan said he would also take this matter under advisement. item.title: Judge dismisses complaint against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden, citing what he said was “weaponization” of President Donald Trump's Justice Department just before the midterm elections. In a scathing, hourlong ruling read from the bench, U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said the investigation that produced the charges against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides was rushed, conducted at the behest of Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel and dogged by “critical mistakes" that require the dismissal of the case. “I am deeply troubled by what has happened here in this case," Faruqui said. “What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.” The ruling may not bring a permanent end to the matter because the Justice Department still has the option of pursuing an indictment, even though it has struggled during the Trump administration to persuade grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one. In the meantime, it nonetheless amounts to a resounding rebuke of a department the judge said could have sought an indictment at any time but instead opted for transparently political purposes to file a criminal complaint in the immediate run-up to Tuesday's midterm voting . “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said, alluding to the proximity of the charges to the elections, which will determine control of Congress for the last two years of the Republican president's second term. Prosecutors had accused the two former FBI officials of falsely downplaying to Congress their knowledge of investigations into President Joe Biden's son and of a laptop the younger Biden dropped off at a computer repair shop in Delaware in 2019. But Faruqui said the Justice Department had failed to establish in its complaint that any statements made during 2023 testimony were intentionally false and had affected lawmakers' investigation of Hunter Biden or that the former officials had any motive to deceive. “Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing" to go on, Faruqui said to establish probable cause needed to affirm the complaint. Lawyers for Floris, who after the ruling hugged supporters outside the courtroom, said the “so-called prosecution was nothing more than a politically motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections." “The charges brought under the clearly discredited authority of the Department of Justice should never have been brought in the first place,” the attorneys said in a statement. The judge identified a political motive and ‘critical mistakes’ The dismissal followed a dramatic three-day hearing last week in which an FBI agent who had been assigned to investigate the case conceded that the inquiry had been regarded around his office as something of a “witch hunt” and that he himself had regarded it as a “huge distraction” from his ordinary case work. The agent, Bryan Witt, said the investigation had been opened one day after a primetime election security speech from Trump in which he rehashed longstanding grievances over his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, a Democrat. He said the investigation was assigned to his Kansas City, Missouri, office and that Patel, a close Trump ally, demanded and received constant updates — something Witt said was unusual. Recounting the pressure to deliver that Witt said he operated under, Faruqui faulted the Trump administration for a rushed investigation that undermined the results. “The rush to charge led to critical mistakes,” he said. Among the errors the magistrate cited was that the complaint said that the two officials had provided sworn testimony to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee when they were not under oath. The judge's concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury's approval. “It is self-evident that the U.S. attorney's office is avoiding taking this case to a grand jury,” Faruqui said. Last week, the Justice Department failed to secure a grand jury indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House staffer who provided dramatic but disputed testimony against Trump before a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection . Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, Faruqui criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before. The case concerns years-old questions about a laptop The case centers on a laptop that the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a Wilmington, Delaware, computer repair shop in 2019. The laptop's existence was publicly disclosed in October 2020 with a New York Post story that reported on some of the laptop's contents. Floris and Benavides were leaders of the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force, or FITF, which was set up to monitor efforts by other countries to meddle in American politics but was disbanded last year by the Trump administration after years of Republican criticism. The Justice Department accused them of falsely downplaying their knowledge of the laptop when they appeared before the House Judiciary Committee as it was conducting its own investigation of Hunter Biden's business dealings. A prosecutor argued last week that the former officials may have had an incentive to minimize their knowledge of the laptop because Joe Biden was president at the time they were questioned and to distance themselves from the fact that the FITF did not publicly correct a narrative from some Democrats and former intelligence officials that the laptop might have been connected to Russian disinformation. Trump’s then-intelligence director, John Ratcliffe , said after the laptop was publicized that there were no signs of foreign involvement. Defense lawyers challenged that characterization. Faruqui said prosecutors had not identified a plausible motive for why the former officials might have made intentionally false statements. item.title: Mother identifies 20-year-old pilot killed in Florida plane crash
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A private jet bound for the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., Sunday afternoon, killing all nine people on board. The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, went down at about 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Dashcam footage posted to social media by an eyewitness showed the aircraft falling toward the ground beside a road and exploding into a fireball, narrowly missing cars and homes. Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" in a post on X , adding: "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost." Air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC captured the crew's comments leading up to the crash. Someone in the cockpit can be heard saying "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, Reuters reported. "We're going to crash into the ground," the person said. The impact left a "massive crater" near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference. About 600 residents were evacuated to two shelters, he said. The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation, and the cause is not yet known. What we know The aircraft crashed in a residential area in Greenacres. Anadolu via Getty Images The Learjet 60 took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. FAA records list the owner as a Delaware corporation. The National Weather Service had a flood watch in effect for the area of the crash, Palm Beach County, through Monday afternoon, with rain expected on and off across South Florida. In air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC, someone in the cockpit said they were "managing the ice" but faced "moderate" turbulence and were seeking "better rides." AP reported the crew also asked to climb. Less than a minute later, the person said "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was suddenly descending at 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person declared an emergency, with the descent rate reaching 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: "We're going to crash into the ground," before reporting the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane began to bank. Flightradar24 data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute. The last words heard from the cockpit were "we're out of time." Accuweather reported that thunderstorms in the area produced heavy rainfall and lightning. The jet is reported to have descended at a peak of 32,000 feet per minute. Anadolu via Getty Images Driver Aki Kuusisto's dashcam footage captured the moment the jet hit the ground. "I heard a whistling noise, a big bang, and I saw a fireball," he told CBS News . "It felt like it was right next to us... you could feel it in the car." Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone injured on the ground. Authorities haven't confirmed what caused the crash or identified the people on board. Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, told the Associated Press that ice and turbulence could have caused the plane to stall. What have officials said? The FAA said the aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when the crash took place. The FAA said it was investigating and would provide further updates. DeSantis told reporters during a Sunday briefing that there were no reports of anyone on the ground being injured despite "a lot of debris" that was strewn over a "pretty significant distance." "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis said. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" and said the FAA and Department of Transportation would be investigating the incident. What did eyewitnesses say? Anthony Blackmon, who lives around 500 feet from the site of the crash, told NBC Miami that debris from the crash struck his home. "Debris was everywhere," he said. "Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire. I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Adam Itayem told WPTV , "It sounded like a loud boom. I thought it was thunder," adding, "I saw a big crater in the ground and water coming out of the crater and a big fire too." "I heard and felt the boom," Andrew Mannino told CNN , saying he saw a "large black cloud immerse in the air," adding, "The power immediately went out and is still out." Around 600 people were evacuated by Palm Beach County authorities while federal officials investigate the crash. "We're waiting for someone to give us answers about what we're going to do, because they're not even letting us into the community to get our clothes," local resident Jesus Solorzano told WPTV. Corteleti said her daughter earned her pilot's license at age 17. Filgueiras had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and was working for a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, according to her mother.
